title: Session fragmentation latency notes
content:
Scratchpad: session fragmentation experiments (quick lab notes)
Owner: Camille Ortiz
Contrib: Ravi (trace collection), Noemi (telemetry)
Date range: 2025-09-11 -> 2026-02-20 (iterative)

Goal
- Understand how short, interleaved sessions (client opens many small contexts rather than one long conversation) affect tail latency and p99 amplification on a 4-GPU shard (A100-ish profile).
- Measure effect of context switch cost (KV cache thrash + kernel rebinds) and short-run scheduling preemption.

Hypothesis
1) Frequent session switches (new ctx every 10–30 tokens) cause p95/p99 to rise due to cache churn and kernel warm-up for different seq-lens.
2) Adaptive batching helps throughput but increases tail latency when sessions are highly fragmented.

Setup 
- Model: small/medium transformer variant (approx 8B) quantized profile q4_2 (representative of a customer workload).
- Fleet: 4x GPUs, 1 serving-process per GPU, runtime tuned with continuous batching enabled.
- Workload generator: synthetic harness mimicking real client populations => mix of long sessions (10%) and fragmented sessions (90%). Fragmented session pattern: 5–20 tokens, pause 50–200ms client think time, then new short request.
- Runs: 6 experiments across different batching timeouts and priority lane settings. Each run = 30 min steady-state after 10 min ramp.

Key metrics captured (per run)
- p50, p90, p95, p99 (server-side response latency), qps, tokens/sec, batch size distribution, KV-cache hit ratio, GPU utilization, preempt count (evictions), context-switch count per second.

Representative run summary (batch_timeout=10ms, adaptive-batching ON, two priority lanes)
- qps: 820 req/s
- tokens/sec: 25k
- mean batch size: 6.1
- p50: 18ms, p90: 62ms, p95: 110ms, p99: 410ms
- KV-cache hit ratio: 0.62
- preempt count (evictions/min): 12
- context-switch events/sec: ~45

Observations
- p99 spikes correlate strongly with moments of high context-switch events (bursts when many short sessions converge).
- Increasing batch timeout (to 25ms) reduces average latency and increases throughput but p99 gets worse: observed p99 ~640ms in one run (batching coalesced more unrelated sessions hence longer queueing for short requests).
- Lowering batch timeout (5ms) reduces p99 but throughput drops ~12% and GPU utilization falls.
- Enabling aggressive KV-cache priming for small contexts improved hit ratio (+0.12) and reduced p99 by ~90ms in targeted runs. That suggests priming small tokens helps amortize the warm cost.
- Preemptions (evictions) were more frequent when the runtime aggressively consolidated batches; eviction cost seemed comparable to a cold-kv fill.

Mini ASCII latency histogram (p99 focus) from one 30-min window (counts in buckets):
0-50ms: |||||||||||||||||||||||| (60%)
50-200ms: |||||||| (24%)
200-500ms: ||| (10%)
>500ms: | (6%)

Quick conclusions
- For highly fragmented session-heavy workloads, set conservative batching (short timeout) and enable KV-cache priming for small contexts to reduce tail. Tradeoff: increased unit cost / slightly lower throughput.
- Introduce short-request fast-path: bypass aggressive coalescing for requests with token_count <= 24 and single-turn flag set. Meant to reduce queuing delay.
- Consider a small per-tenant soft-cache (LRU of recent small context keys) to minimize eviction overhead for frequently returning micro-sessions.

Action items / TODOs
- A1: Run the same suite with 8x GPUs / multi-process-per-GPU arrangement to check whether cross-process isolation reduces p99 (assigned to Ravi) — due 2026-03-05.
- A2: Prototype fast-path gating condition in runtime (PR draft linked above) and run AB test against current strategy (Noemi).
- A3: Add trace markers to capture exact timeline between batch formation and KV-cache hit/miss to quantify eviction vs coldfill cost (small change to tracer instrumentation).

Open questions
- How much of the p99 is networking jitter vs runtime scheduling? Need to replay traces with deterministic network delay to isolate.
- Is per-tenant soft-cache worth memory overhead at scale? Need memory-cost/benefit sim.

Notes to self
- Keep the synthetic harness reproducible: commit seeds and harness config to GH before further runs.
- When sharing results put a short deck (3 slides) for product: describe recommendation (fast-path + priming), expected cost delta, and rollback plan.

Related links
- JIRA-ENG-8421: session fragmentation story
- PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/614 (fast-path prototype)
- Slack thread: #perf-latency "session-frag traces" (link pinned)

End of scratchpad.
